newsitem.title: USA: More Canada gas seen flowing to growing US market.
newsitem.headline: More Canada gas seen flowing to growing US market.

text.p: Canada's natural gas exports to the U.S. will rise significantly over the next few years but are unlikely to boost their current share of the giant U.S. market, industry officials said.

"In terms of volume, we are certainly anticipating Canadian supplies to continue to grow. In terms of a percentage of the market it is not quite as clear," said Charlotte LeGates, spokeswoman for the U.S.-based Natural Gas Supply Association.

Despite growing volumes from planned pipeline projects from Canada, the country's share of gas supply is expected to remain at 12 to 14 percent of U.S. needs due to growing U.S. gas consumption, the officials said.

Figures released last week by the Canadian government body Statistics Canada showed Canadian gas exports to the U.S. rose 8.2 percent in January to a record high of 7.7 billion cubic metres (273 billion cubic feet).
In 1996, Canada sent about 2.8 trillion cubic feet of gas to the U.S., or about 13 percent of total 1996 U.S. gas use of about 22 trillion cubic feet.

Annual Canadian exports of gas to the U.S. should reach about 3.76 trillion cubic feet by 2010, which is expected to make up about 14 percent of U.S. consumption, according to Roland George, vice president of natural gas research for the Canadian Energy Research Institute.
"There isn't much more room for growth in terms of (Canadian) share of the U.S. marketplace," George said.

Pipeline projects like the proposed $2.6 billion (C$3.6 billion) Alliance Pipeline, to bring northern Canadian natural gas to Chicago, are among those that will boost Canadian exports to the U.S., the officials said.
The Alliance Pipeline project, planned to start up in late 1999, includes such backers as Gulf Canada Resources Ltd and Chevron Corp unit Chevron Canada Resources Ltd.
The proposed pipeline would have the capacity to move over 1.3 billion cubic feet per day of Canadian gas into the U.S.
"We see (U.S.) demand growing significantly, but we don't see the Canadian share growing," said Brian White, director of natural gas transportation for the American Gas Association (AGA).

"(The gas producing Canadian province of) Alberta is so far from the primary U.S. consuming regions -- that's the Canadian disadvantage," White said, adding "the Canadian advantage is that it is the lowest cost supply basin."
